contradictions.question: Has anyone ever ascended into heaven?
contradictions.summary: John 3:13 has Jesus say flatly that no human has ascended into heaven except the Son of Man. Genesis 5:24 and Hebrews 11:5 say Enoch was taken by God — and 2 Kings 2:11 has Elijah taken up in a whirlwind. The Johannine claim contradicts the texts the Johannine author would have known.
contradictions.commentary:
Take John 3:13 at face value: "No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man." That is a universal negation. Genesis 5:24 says of Enoch, "God took him," and Hebrews 11:5 spells out the interpretation explicitly — "Enoch was taken so that he did not experience death." 2 Kings 2:11 adds Elijah going up by a whirlwind into heaven. So either Enoch and Elijah went up or John 3:13 is wrong. Pick one.

The standard apologist move here is to distinguish ascending "under one's own power" from being "taken up" by God, or to argue John means no one has ascended and returned to reveal heavenly things except Jesus. D.A. Carson and Andreas Kostenberger both lean on this revelatory-disclosure reading. The problem is that the text doesn't say that. It says no one has ascended. And the Second Temple Jewish tradition that John inherits — 1 Enoch, 2 Enoch, the Apocalypse of Abraham, the Testament of Levi — is built on exactly the premise that Enoch and Elijah did ascend and brought back heavenly knowledge. James VanderKam has documented this for decades. John's claim only works if you erase the entire apocalyptic tradition the Fourth Gospel is otherwise dialoguing with.

Raymond Brown, in the Anchor Bible commentary, concedes that the verse is polemical — it's aimed at Jewish apocalyptic claims of mystical heavenly ascent, and it deliberately denies what those traditions affirmed. That's not harmonization. That's admitting the contradiction is theological, with the Johannine author rewriting earlier Jewish claims to elevate Jesus as the sole revealer. Bart Ehrman and Maurice Casey have argued the same — John is asserting Christological exclusivity by contradicting the older texts on purpose.

Verdict: the contradiction is real and the Fourth Gospel knows it. The harmonization only survives if you read "ascended" with a custom restrictive meaning the text doesn't provide. The plain reading collides with Genesis 5, Hebrews 11, and 2 Kings 2.

contradictions.question: Is it OK to call someone father?
contradictions.summary: The Decalogue commands honoring your father (Exodus 20:12, Deuteronomy 5:16) and Paul reaffirms it in Ephesians 6:2. Jesus in Matthew 23:9 says "call no man your father upon the earth, for one is your Father, which is in heaven." The commandments require recognizing earthly fathers; the Matthean Jesus forbids the title.
contradictions.commentary:
The fifth commandment, repeated in both Exodus and Deuteronomy and then quoted back by Ephesians as "the first commandment with promise," tells you to honor your father. To do that, you have to identify someone as your father. Matthew 23:9 says don't do that on earth. Read at face value, the Matthean Jesus has just contradicted Sinai.

The standard harmonization, championed by R.T. France and Craig Blomberg, is that Matthew 23 is about titles of religious authority — "Father" as honorific for rabbis or teachers, not biological parentage. France in the NICNT argues the passage targets pretensions of spiritual paternity, not domestic vocabulary. That reading has some traction. The immediate context in Matthew 23 is rabbinic title-claiming ("rabbi," "teacher"), so "father" likely belongs to the same semantic field of religious honorifics. Davies and Allison in the ICC concede the absolute reading is overstated and that the polemic is against pretenders to religious authority.

But here's the issue. The text says "call no man your father upon the earth." It doesn't say "call no man rabbi-father." The Matthean author chose a universal formulation, and the burden of restricting it falls on the apologist. Ulrich Luz, in the Hermeneia volume, notes that Matthew is deliberately maximalist in his anti-hierarchical rhetoric — the saying functions to flatten ecclesial structure, not just to forbid one specific title. And the early church didn't read it as Catholic-priest-only either; the Didache and Justin Martyr struggle with what "father" applies to.

The contradiction is therefore real on a plain reading and softened only on a contextual reading that requires importing restrictions Matthew didn't write. The fifth commandment requires the cognitive act of identifying someone as "father." Matthew 23:9 forbids that cognitive act on earth. The harmonization works if you accept the apologist's restrictive gloss. The face-value reading doesn't. Take your pick.

contradictions.question: Should we rend our clothes?
contradictions.summary: 2 Kings 22:19 and the parallel 2 Chronicles 34:27 record God praising Josiah for rending his clothes; Ecclesiastes 3:7 lists a "time to rend." Joel 2:13 calls for rending hearts "not your garments," and 2 Kings 5:8 has Elisha rebuke the king of Israel for tearing his clothes. The texts cannot agree on whether the practice is virtue or vanity.
contradictions.commentary:
The Deuteronomistic Historian in 2 Kings 22 and the Chronicler in 2 Chronicles 34 both highlight Josiah's clothes-rending as evidence of a tender heart — and God explicitly says so. Ecclesiastes naturalizes the practice as a culturally appropriate response to grief. Joel 2:13 then reverses the polarity: "Rend your hearts, not your garments," framing the physical act as a substitute for genuine repentance. And in 2 Kings 5:8, Elisha is annoyed at the king of Israel for rending his clothes over Naaman's letter, treating it as a faithless overreaction.

Apologists like Gleason Archer and Norman Geisler argue these aren't contradictions because the texts target different intentions — sincere mourning is approved, performative mourning is condemned. There's truth to that. Joel 2 is clearly polemicizing against ritual without repentance, not banning the practice outright. The Hebrew construction in Joel 2:13 is the classic "not X but Y" idiom that Hebraists like James Barr have shown can mean "not merely X but rather Y," so it's possible to read it as comparative rather than exclusive.

But that defense only goes so far. The texts present mixed normative valences depending on author and period. Pre-exilic Deuteronomistic theology valorized the act as religious sincerity. Post-exilic prophetic literature — Joel, Isaiah 58 — increasingly interiorizes ritual, downgrading the physical expressions. This is exactly the kind of theological development Marvin Sweeney and Hans Walter Wolff track in their work on prophetic critique of cult. The contradiction is real at the surface level and resolved only if you accept that the canon contains theologically evolving voices that don't speak with one mouth.

Verdict: not a hard logical contradiction once you grant intent-distinctions, but a clear case of competing canonical attitudes. The apologetic harmonization works at the cost of admitting the texts represent different theological priorities.

contradictions.question: Did God give Gehazi leprosy?
contradictions.summary: 2 Kings 5:27 has Elisha curse Gehazi with leprosy permanently — "unto thee and unto thy seed forever" — and the narrator says Gehazi went out "a leper as white as snow." 2 Kings 8:4 then has Gehazi conversing face-to-face with the king of Israel, which the Levitical purity laws would have made impossible for an actual leper.
contradictions.commentary:
2 Kings 5:27 closes Naaman's healing story with a vicious narrative reversal: Naaman is cleansed, Gehazi is cursed, and the curse is hereditary and perpetual. Three chapters later, 2 Kings 8:4 has the king of Israel chatting with Gehazi, asking him to recount Elisha's deeds. Under Leviticus 13-14, a person designated "leprous" — the Hebrew is tsara'at, a broader skin-disease category than modern leprosy — would be ritually quarantined outside the camp/city and barred from royal proximity. So either Gehazi was healed off-screen, the law was being ignored, or one of the narratives doesn't know the other.

The apologist responses, from Archer through John Walton, fall into two camps. First, the chronological-shuffling defense: 2 Kings 8 may narrate events from before chapter 5, since Deuteronomistic compilers don't always order pericopae chronologically. Mordechai Cogan and Hayim Tadmor in the Anchor Bible volume note that 2 Kings 4-8 is a loose anthology of Elisha legends, not a strict chronological history. That's a real point. Second, the healing-implied defense: God may have lifted the curse off-screen, even though the text gives no indication of this.

The critical-scholarly read, anchored by Burke Long in his FOTL Kings volume and Marvin Sweeney in his OTL commentary, is that 2 Kings is a redacted collage of prophetic legend cycles drawn from independent oral traditions. The Gehazi-leprosy story and the Gehazi-at-court story almost certainly come from separate cycles. The redactor preserved both without fully integrating them. This is the same phenomenon you see with Saul meeting David multiple times for the first time in 1 Samuel.

Verdict: the chronological-shuffling defense is plausible on its own terms but admits the text is non-sequential, which means the canonical narrative is internally inconsistent even if individual episodes can be saved by repositioning. The contradiction stands as evidence for source-critical layering, not for a deliberate authorial sequence.

contradictions.question: Who was Athaliah's father?
contradictions.summary: 2 Kings 8:26 and 2 Chronicles 22:2 call Athaliah "the daughter of Omri." 2 Kings 8:18 and 2 Chronicles 21:6 call her "the daughter of Ahab." Omri and Ahab are father and son — one cannot biologically be her father if the other is.
contradictions.commentary:
The simplest reading: 2 Kings 8:26 makes Athaliah Omri's daughter, and three verses earlier 2 Kings 8:18 makes her Ahab's daughter. Same chapter, two different fathers. The Chronicler reproduces the same conflict in 21:6 versus 22:2.

Apologists like Gleason Archer and Edwin Thiele standardize the harmonization here: "daughter" in Biblical Hebrew (bat) can mean granddaughter or female descendant, so "daughter of Omri" might just mean "of the Omride dynasty." Archer's Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties leans on this hard. There's lexicographic support — Hebrew kinship terms are notoriously elastic, and bat does extend to female descendants generally. So Omri is the dynastic ancestor and Ahab is the biological father.

The critical-scholarly view, articulated by Mordechai Cogan in his Anchor Bible volume on I Kings and reaffirmed by Steven McKenzie, is that this elastic reading is technically possible but conceals a real historical question. Some scholars — Hayim Tadmor and Cogan together in the II Kings volume — go further and suggest Athaliah may actually have been Omri's daughter, a sister of Ahab rather than his daughter, married off to consolidate the Omride-Davidic alliance during Jehoshaphat's reign. If so, the "daughter of Ahab" notice is a later redactional confusion. Lester Grabbe and Baruch Halpern have explored similar scenarios.

Either way, the harmonization works only by invoking lexical flexibility that the text doesn't signal. The natural reading of "daughter of Ahab" in a single narrative arc is biological daughter. The Deuteronomist almost certainly understood her as Ahab's daughter; the Omride dynastic label may be the looser usage. But the texts do not stipulate this, and the contradiction at the surface level is real. Take your pick — granddaughter-elastic-Hebrew or genuine redactional inconsistency. Either way, the plain-reading harmonization fails.

contradictions.question: How old was Ahaziah when he began to reign?
contradictions.summary: 2 Kings 8:26 says Ahaziah was 22 when he began to reign. 2 Chronicles 22:2 says he was 42. Since his father Jehoram died at age 40 (2 Chronicles 21:20), the Chronicles figure makes Ahaziah older than his own father.
contradictions.commentary:
This is one of the cleanest numerical contradictions in the Hebrew Bible. 2 Kings 8:26 puts Ahaziah at 22. 2 Chronicles 22:2 puts him at 42. The arithmetic problem compounds: 2 Chronicles 21:5 and 21:20 say Jehoram was 32 when he began to reign and reigned 8 years, dying at 40. If his son Ahaziah was 42, the son outlived his father by two years before the father died. Mathematically impossible.

Apologists across the spectrum — Archer, Keil and Delitzsch, the older Geisler-Howe handbook — converge on the scribal-error explanation. The Hebrew numerical system, especially in pre-Masoretic transmission, used letter-based number representations that were easily corrupted. Archer argues 22 is original (2 Kings) and 42 is a transmission error (2 Chronicles). The LXX of 2 Chronicles 22:2 reads 22, supporting this. Syriac Peshitta and some Lucianic recensions also read 20 or 22.

This is one of those cases where critical scholarship and apologists actually agree on the diagnosis — scribal corruption — but disagree on what it implies. Ralph Klein in the Hermeneia 2 Chronicles volume, Sara Japhet in OTL, and Raymond Dillard in the WBC 2 Chronicles volume all acknowledge the textual error. The critical scholar's question is what this implies about inerrancy. If the autograph of 2 Chronicles 22:2 said 22 and a copyist wrote 42, the canonical text now contains an error. The Masoretic Text is what's canonical for Protestants. Anneli Aejmelaeus's work on the Old Greek of Samuel-Kings has documented dozens of similar numerical divergences between MT and LXX.

Verdict: a real, conceded contradiction in the received text. The harmonization is textual-critical — appeal to a corrected reading — and it works at the cost of acknowledging the received Masoretic text contains transmission errors. That's not a problem for critical scholarship. It is a problem for inerrancy as commonly defined.

contradictions.question: When did Ahaziah begin to reign?
contradictions.summary: 2 Kings 8:25 dates Ahaziah's accession to the twelfth year of Joram king of Israel. 2 Kings 9:29 dates the same accession to the eleventh year of Joram. The two notices contradict each other within the same book, four chapters apart.
contradictions.commentary:
Same king, same accession event, two different synchronisms, sitting in adjacent chapters of the same composition. 2 Kings 8:25 says twelfth year of Joram. 2 Kings 9:29 says eleventh year of Joram. There is no theological subtlety here. It is a chronological inconsistency.

Apologetic responses fall into two camps. Edwin Thiele, whose chronological reconstruction has dominated conservative evangelical scholarship since the 1950s, argues that the two notices reflect different reckoning systems — one using accession-year reckoning (where a king's first partial year counts as year zero of his own reign) and another using non-accession-year reckoning. By coordinating Judah's and Israel's distinct calendars, Thiele extracts an internally consistent timeline. Andrew Steinmann has updated and refined Thiele's framework. Within their system, the apparent contradiction dissolves into different but compatible counting conventions.

This is genuinely ingenious work, but critical scholars from John Bright through Mordechai Cogan and Hayim Tadmor in the Anchor Bible volume have pushed back hard. The Thiele system requires assuming changes in reckoning convention that the text never signals, multiple coregencies the text never mentions, and arithmetic gymnastics that often run to coincidence. Cogan and Tadmor flatly call 2 Kings 9:29 a redactional gloss — a later editor's note that contradicts the earlier 8:25 figure and was never reconciled. Marvin Sweeney in OTL takes the same position. The simpler explanation is that the Deuteronomistic Historian was working from independent source documents with inconsistent dates and didn't smooth them out.

This is the apologist playbook page one: when a contradiction shows up in numbers, invoke an unstated reckoning convention that just happens to dissolve it. The harmonization is unfalsifiable because there's no independent evidence the convention shifts occurred. Critical scholarship treats these synchronisms as redactional artifacts, not historical data.

Verdict: a contradiction in the received text, harmonized only by invoking an elaborate chronological scheme the text doesn't author. Parsimoniously, this is a redactional inconsistency.

contradictions.question: Did God commend or condemn Jehu for the killings at Jezreel?
contradictions.summary: 2 Kings 9:6-8 has God commission Jehu to wipe out the house of Ahab, an instruction Jehu carries out with extreme violence at Jezreel. Hosea 1:4 has the same God announce he will avenge "the blood of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu" — meaning he will punish Jehu's dynasty for the very killings he ordered.
contradictions.commentary:
This is one of the sharpest moral-theological contradictions in the Hebrew Bible. The Deuteronomistic narrator in 2 Kings 9 has Yahweh anoint Jehu through a prophet of Elisha and explicitly command him to slaughter Ahab's house. Jehu obeys: he kills Joram of Israel, Ahaziah of Judah, Jezebel, the seventy sons of Ahab, Ahaziah's relatives, and the prophets of Baal. The narrator endorses this in 2 Kings 10:30 — "because thou hast done well in executing that which is right in mine eyes."

Then Hosea 1:4 happens. The prophet Hosea — writing roughly a century later — names his son Jezreel and declares that Yahweh will "avenge the blood of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu, and will cause to cease the kingdom of the house of Israel." The same God who ordered the killings now treats them as bloodguilt requiring vengeance.

The apologist harmonization, defended by Hans Walter Wolff cautiously and by Duane Garrett more forcefully in the NAC Hosea volume, draws a distinction between the act commanded and the manner executed. Jehu was commissioned to remove Ahab's house. He was not commissioned to massacre with the brutality and overreach he displayed — killing Ahaziah, all the prophets, and beyond what divine sanction covered. Hosea condemns the excess, not the obedience.

That reading has some weight. Jehu did exceed his mandate. But it leaves a problem: 2 Kings 10:30 explicitly says Yahweh approved Jehu's conduct as "right." If the manner was wrong, the Deuteronomist didn't get the memo. Critical scholars from Wolff to Marvin Sweeney to Francis Andersen and David Noel Freedman in the AB Hosea read this as competing theological evaluations from different periods. The Deuteronomist celebrated Jehu's purge as covenant fidelity; Hosea, a century into the consequences, read the same purge as bloody dynastic crime requiring divine reckoning. Same act, contradictory canonical verdicts.

Verdict: the surface contradiction is real and the manner-vs-mandate harmonization works only by ignoring 2 Kings 10:30. Critical scholarship treats this as evidence of competing theological perspectives within the canon — not a logical error so much as a moral evolution.

contradictions.question: Where was Joash buried?
contradictions.summary: 2 Kings 12:21 says Joash was buried with his fathers in the city of David — the standard royal-burial formula. 2 Chronicles 24:25 says he was buried in the city of David but explicitly "not in the sepulchres of the kings," because of his apostasy. The Chronicler is rewriting the Kings account to insert a posthumous demerit.
contradictions.commentary:
The Deuteronomistic Historian in 2 Kings 12 reports Joash's death and burial in standard royal terms: he slept with his fathers, was buried with them in the city of David, and Amaziah his son reigned in his stead. End of pericope. The Chronicler, looking at the same king, makes a deliberate alteration. 2 Chronicles 24:25 keeps "the city of David" but inserts the qualifier "but they buried him not in the sepulchres of the kings."

Apologists like Eugene Merrill and Andrew Hill argue these can be reconciled — the Kings phrasing is general, the Chronicles phrasing is specific. Buried in the city of David (general truth) but not specifically in the royal sepulchres (specific detail). On the surface that works. "With his fathers" in 2 Kings can mean "in his ancestral city" without specifying which tomb.

But the harmonization misses what's interesting here. Sara Japhet in the OTL Chronicles volume, Steven McKenzie in the Abingdon OT Commentary, and Raymond Dillard in the Word Biblical Commentary all read the Chronicler's alteration as theologically motivated. The Chronicler is famous for adjusting Kings material to fit a strict retribution theology — good kings prosper, bad kings die badly. Joash starts well, restores the temple, then apostatizes after Jehoiada's death and is assassinated by his own servants. The Chronicler signals the divine displeasure by denying him royal burial. This is the same move he makes with Jehoram (2 Chronicles 21:20), Uzziah (2 Chronicles 26:23), and Ahaz (2 Chronicles 28:27).

Gary Knoppers and Ralph Klein both classify this as Chronistic redactional theology, not historical correction. The Chronicler doesn't have access to new information; he's editorializing on the Kings narrative. The harmonization works as a logical possibility but ignores the obvious literary pattern. The Chronicler systematically rewrites royal burials to match his theological grid.

Verdict: technically harmonizable as general-vs-specific, but the critical reading exposes the alteration as a deliberate theological rewrite. The two texts contradict not at the level of a brute fact about Joash's tomb but at the level of canonical evaluation of his reign.

contradictions.question: When did Jehoash become king of Israel?
contradictions.summary: 2 Kings 13:10 dates Jehoash of Israel's accession to the thirty-seventh year of Joash of Judah. The first cited passage (2 Kings 13:1) gives Jehoahaz's accession in Joash's twenty-third year and a seventeen-year reign, totaling forty years before Jehoash takes over. The two computations cannot both be correct.
contradictions.commentary:
The accession of Jehoash king of Israel sits in 2 Kings 13:10 at year 37 of Joash king of Judah. Run the numbers from 2 Kings 13:1 instead: Jehoahaz (Jehoash's father) takes the Israelite throne in year 23 of Joash and reigns 17 years. 23 + 17 = 40. So Jehoash of Israel should accede in Joash of Judah's 40th year, not his 37th. Three-year discrepancy embedded in the same chapter.

The Thiele framework — promoted by Edwin Thiele in The Mysterious Numbers of the Hebrew Kings and elaborated by Leslie McFall and Andrew Steinmann — handles this by positing a coregency. Jehoash, on this view, was made co-regent with Jehoahaz around year 37 and acceded solo around year 40. The differing dates record different milestones in the same reign. This is technically possible and Thiele applies the same coregency-machine to dozens of similar problems.

The critical-scholarly view, articulated by Mordechai Cogan and Hayim Tadmor in the AB volume and by John Bright in his classic History of Israel, is that the coregency hypothesis is essentially unfalsifiable. Coregencies aren't mentioned in the text. They're constructed retroactively whenever the numbers don't add up. When you need them, you posit them. Cogan and Tadmor categorize 13:10 as one of several synchronisms that resist Thielian reconciliation without ad hoc adjustments.

Anneli Aejmelaeus's work on the Old Greek of Samuel-Kings shows that the LXX preserves dozens of variant numerical readings that suggest the Hebrew tradition itself was unstable on these chronological details. The Deuteronomistic Historian was working from regnal lists of uncertain accuracy and didn't always reconcile them.

Note on the question: the first answer cites 2 Kings 13:1 — which records Jehoahaz's accession, not Jehoash's. The contradiction is real but indirect: 13:1's data (year 23 + 17 years reign) implies Jehoash should accede in year 40, which contradicts 13:10's explicit year 37. So the question framing requires arithmetic to surface the contradiction.

Verdict: a numerical contradiction in the received text, harmonized only by invoking unattested coregencies. Critical scholarship treats it as a redactional inconsistency stemming from unreconciled source lists.

contradictions.question: Who was Uzziah's father?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 1:8 puts "Joram begat Ozias [Uzziah]" in Jesus' genealogy. 1 Chronicles 3:11-12 lists the actual lineage as Joram, Ahaziah, Joash, Amaziah, Azariah (= Uzziah). Matthew has skipped three generations.
contradictions.commentary:
Matthew's genealogy in chapter 1 is constructed to fit a 14-14-14 generational pattern (Matthew 1:17). To make the numbers work, the author of Matthew telescopes the Davidic line by dropping three kings — Ahaziah, Joash, and Amaziah — between Joram and Uzziah/Azariah. 1 Chronicles 3:11-12 preserves the full line. So Matthew's "Joram begat Ozias" is wrong if "begat" means biological paternity.

The standard apologetic move, defended by Craig Blomberg and Donald Hagner, is that the Greek verb gennao ("begat") in Hellenistic Jewish genealogies can mean "was the ancestor of" rather than "was the immediate father of." Matthew is constructing a theological genealogy, not a biological pedigree, and the dropped generations are deliberate stylization for the 14-14-14 schema. R.T. France in the NICNT and W.D. Davies and Dale Allison in the ICC both accept this as the standard explanation.

There's lexical and rhetorical support for this. Hebrew yalad and Greek gennao both admit broader genealogical use. Genesis 46:8-27 uses similar telescoping. Some apologists go further and argue Matthew dropped the names of the kings descended from Athaliah's bloodline because Athaliah was an Omride and the dynasty was theologically tainted — Raymond Brown explores this possibility in The Birth of the Messiah but doesn't endorse it. Brown himself reads the omission as numerological convenience and treats the resulting genealogy as historically inaccurate but theologically purposive.

The critical-scholarly question isn't whether Matthew can be defended on lexical grounds — he can. It's whether Matthew was aware he was contradicting 1 Chronicles, or whether he was working from a different genealogical source. Bart Ehrman has argued the latter — Matthew likely had access to genealogical traditions independent of the Chronicler's list. Either way, Matthew 1:8 cannot be reconciled with 1 Chronicles 3 if "begat" is read as biological paternity. The contradiction dissolves only under the looser lexical reading, which is itself an admission that biblical genealogies don't function the way modern genealogies do.

Verdict: a real contradiction in literal terms, dissolved by accepting that genealogical "begat" is elastic. The apologist harmonization works at the cost of conceding the historicity of Matthew's chain.

contradictions.question: Does God allow pregnant women to be ripped apart?
contradictions.summary: Hosea 13:16 has Yahweh announce that Samaria's pregnant women "shall be ripped up" as judgment — divine sanction on the act. Amos 1:13 has Yahweh condemn the Ammonites for ripping up the pregnant women of Gilead. The same act receives canonical approval and canonical condemnation depending on who is doing it to whom.
contradictions.commentary:
Hosea 13:16 (Hebrew Bible 14:1) prophesies that Samaria's punishment will include infants dashed in pieces and pregnant women ripped open. The text frames this as divine judgment — Yahweh announcing what he will bring on his own people for rebellion. Amos 1:13 condemns the Ammonites for doing the same thing to Gilead's pregnant women in war. The verb across both passages is the same root b-q-' — to cleave open.

The apologetic harmonization, articulated by Douglas Stuart in the Word Biblical Commentary and Duane Garrett in the NAC, distinguishes between divine permission and divine endorsement. God permits or even prophetically announces atrocities as judgment without morally endorsing the perpetrators. The Ammonites in Amos 1 were acting out of "enlarging their border" — pure imperial expansion, not divine commission — so their motive deserves condemnation. The Assyrians (the implied agents in Hosea 13) are God's "rod of anger" (Isaiah 10:5), which the prophets occasionally acknowledge.

That distinction has some traction. Hosea 13 doesn't explicitly say God commands the act — it announces the act as the consequence of judgment. Amos 1 condemns Ammonite motive. Stuart and Garrett package this neatly as a doctrine of divine permission distinct from divine moral approval.

Here's where the critical reading bites back. James Crenshaw and Hans Walter Wolff both note that the Hosea oracle uses first-person divine speech in 13:8-16 — "I will tear them open," "I will be unto them as a lion." The prophet attributes the violence directly to Yahweh, not to an Assyrian instrument. The agent and the moral evaluator are the same speaker. Eric Seibert in The Violence of Scripture argues the canonical text shows competing prophetic traditions — some prophets envisioned Yahweh as direct perpetrator of war atrocities against Israel, others as moral judge of nations that committed those atrocities. The two views were preserved together without reconciliation.

Verdict: the divine-permission distinction softens the contradiction but doesn't dissolve it. The two texts attribute the same act to different moral evaluations depending on the perpetrator's identity. The plain reading of Hosea 13 has God as agent of an atrocity that the plain reading of Amos 1 has him punishing. Take your pick — selective divine permission or competing prophetic theologies.

contradictions.question: How long did Jotham reign?
contradictions.summary: 2 Kings 15:32-33 says Jotham reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem. 2 Kings 15:30 references "the twentieth year of Jotham," implying his reign extended at least four years beyond the official total. The book of Kings cannot agree with itself on Jotham's regnal length.
contradictions.commentary:
2 Kings 15:33 gives the formal regnal notice: Jotham reigned 16 years. Two verses earlier, 2 Kings 15:30 dates Hoshea's accession in Israel to the twentieth year of Jotham. If Jotham only reigned 16 years, there can be no twentieth year of Jotham.

The Thiele harmonization handles this with — surprise — another coregency. On Thiele's reconstruction, Jotham was made co-regent with his leprous father Uzziah/Azariah around 750 BCE and his official 16-year reign overlapped with a longer period during which his "years" were counted in synchronisms with Israel. Year 20 of Jotham, in this scheme, falls during Ahaz's reign and is counted retrospectively from Jotham's coregency rather than his sole reign. Andrew Steinmann has elaborated this.

Mordechai Cogan and Hayim Tadmor in the AB II Kings volume call this what it is: a redactional inconsistency. The synchronism in 15:30 is almost certainly a late editorial gloss attempting to coordinate Israelite and Judean regnal data, and it conflicts with the formal notice in 15:33. Marvin Sweeney in OTL reaches the same conclusion. The Deuteronomistic editor or a later glossator inserted the twentieth-year reference without reconciling it with the official length. This is a classic case of source data preserved without smoothing.

The apologist response works only if you accept the coregency machinery — and the text never describes Jotham as co-regent with anyone. The textual datum is bare: 16 years officially, year 20 referenced.

Verdict: a numerical contradiction harmonized only by importing an unattested coregency. The plain text gives Jotham 16 years and then references his 20th. Both can't be true without a hypothetical reckoning convention the text doesn't author.

contradictions.question: Was Ahaz buried with his fathers?
contradictions.summary: 2 Kings 16:20 says Ahaz "was buried with his fathers in the city of David" — the standard royal-burial formula. 2 Chronicles 28:27 says he was buried in Jerusalem "but they brought him not into the sepulchres of the kings of Israel." The Chronicler has rewritten the Deuteronomistic burial notice to add a posthumous demerit for Ahaz's apostasy.
contradictions.commentary:
Same pattern as the Joash burial contradiction at id 289. The Deuteronomistic Historian buries Ahaz "with his fathers in the city of David" — the formula that signals dynastic continuity and royal honor. The Chronicler keeps the city-of-David part but explicitly excludes Ahaz from the royal sepulchres. The verbal divergence is small. The theological implication is enormous.

Apologists like Eugene Merrill argue this is general-vs-specific again — buried in the broader royal precinct but not in the inner kings' tombs. Andrew Hill in his NIVAC Chronicles volume accepts this gloss. R.K. Harrison's older Introduction to the Old Testament defends similar harmonizations across the Kings-Chronicles burial notices.

The critical reading, championed by Sara Japhet in OTL, Ralph Klein in Hermeneia, and Raymond Dillard with Martin Selman together, treats this as another instance of Chronistic redactional theology. The Chronicler systematically denies royal burial to kings he evaluates negatively — Jehoram, Joash, Uzziah, Ahaz. He's making the burial location track moral evaluation. Steven McKenzie and Gary Knoppers both treat this as a clear pattern of theological rewriting, not the recovery of independent historical information.

This is the apologist playbook again: harmonize at the surface level by inserting a distinction the texts don't actually mark, and ignore the obvious literary pattern that explains the divergence. The Chronicler isn't supplementing Kings with new factual data. He's editorializing on the Kings narrative by adjusting the burial notices to encode his retribution theology.

Verdict: technically harmonizable as general-vs-specific, but the harmonization ignores the literary evidence that the Chronicler deliberately rewrote the burial notice for theological effect. Two texts, two evaluations of Ahaz's death, presented as factual claims that don't sit together.

contradictions.question: Who was the best king?
contradictions.summary: 2 Kings 18:5 says of Hezekiah that "after him was none like him among all the kings of Judah, nor any that were before him." 2 Kings 23:25 says of Josiah, "like unto him was there no king before him... neither after him arose there any like him." Both can't be uniquely unparalleled.
contradictions.commentary:
The Deuteronomistic Historian gives the same incomparability formula to two different Judahite kings, six chapters apart. Hezekiah is uniquely the greatest in 2 Kings 18:5. Josiah is uniquely the greatest in 2 Kings 23:25. Mathematically, set theoretically, logically — both cannot be the singular best. The formula is exclusive on its face: "none like him" before or after.

Apologetic harmonizers like Iain Provan and Walter Kaiser argue the praise is qualified by different criteria. Hezekiah is uniquely praised for trusting Yahweh ("he trusted in the LORD God of Israel"). Josiah is uniquely praised for turning to Yahweh with all his heart, soul, and might "according to all the law of Moses." Two different superlatives, two different evaluative axes. So Hezekiah was the best at trust; Josiah was the best at Torah-fidelity. They coexist without contradiction.

That reading has some legitimate textual support — the praise formulae are differently scoped. But Marvin Sweeney in his OTL volume and Choon-Leong Seow in the New Interpreter's Bible both push back. The incomparability formula in both verses is unqualified — "none like him" full stop. The reading that limits each praise to a different sphere is reader-imposed restriction, not text-marked. Iain Provan, who's normally a more conservative reader, concedes in his 1 & 2 Kings commentary that the formulae are awkwardly parallel and likely reflect different Deuteronomistic redactors emphasizing different ideal kings.

The critical-scholarly consensus, traceable from Martin Noth through Frank Cross's double-redaction hypothesis, is that the Deuteronomistic History was edited in stages — a pre-exilic Josianic edition and an exilic revision. The pre-exilic edition celebrated Josiah as the climactic ideal king. The exilic edition needed to explain why Josiah didn't actually save Judah from destruction, so it elevated Hezekiah retroactively. The two superlatives are vestiges of two redactional layers.

Verdict: contradiction at the plain-reading level, softened by qualified-superlative apologetics, but better explained by source-critical layering. The Deuteronomist couldn't decide who his hero was and the canon preserved both.

contradictions.question: Why did God turn the sundial back ten degrees?
contradictions.summary: 2 Kings 20:7-11 makes the sundial sign about confirming Hezekiah's healing from a boil. Isaiah 38:4-8 (in the parallel narrative) makes it about confirming the promise of fifteen additional years and deliverance from Assyria. The two accounts of the same prodigy assign different referents to the sign.
contradictions.commentary:
The two parallel narratives — 2 Kings 20 and Isaiah 38 — share most of the Hezekiah-illness pericope but diverge on what the sundial reversal signifies. In 2 Kings 20:7-11, Isaiah applies a fig poultice to the boil, Hezekiah recovers, and then Hezekiah asks for a sign that he will be healed and go up to the temple on the third day. The shadow-reversal is the sign of healing. In Isaiah 38:4-8, the narrative reorganizes: God promises fifteen additional years AND deliverance of the city from Assyria, and the shadow-reversal confirms that combined promise.

Apologists like John Oswalt in his NICOT Isaiah volume argue these aren't contradictory but complementary — the sign was multipurpose. It confirmed both healing and deliverance simultaneously. Edward J. Young's older Isaiah commentary makes the same move. The two narrators just emphasize different aspects of the same multi-referent miracle.

That works only if you ignore the actual narrative sequencing. In 2 Kings 20:7-8 the healing comes BEFORE the sign-request — Hezekiah is healed and then asks for confirmation that he'll go to the temple. The sign retroactively confirms an already-completed healing. In Isaiah 38 the sequence is reordered: the promise comes first, the sign confirms it, and the healing follows. Joseph Blenkinsopp in the AB Isaiah 1-39 volume and Brevard Childs in the OTL Isaiah commentary both note this is editorial rearrangement, not just different emphasis.

Hans Wildberger in the Continental Commentary volumes argues persuasively that Isaiah 38-39 was redacted into the Isaiah scroll later as a kind of historical appendix and the redactor reshaped the Kings material to serve different theological purposes — specifically, framing the deliverance of Jerusalem from Sennacherib as the central concern. The 2 Kings version preserves an older, simpler healing narrative.

Verdict: the contradiction is at the level of narrative structure and sign-referent, not just emphasis. The complementary-multi-purpose harmonization works only by flattening the editorial differences. Critical scholarship treats these as redactional reshaping of a shared source.

contradictions.question: How did King Josiah die?
contradictions.summary: Huldah's oracle in 2 Kings 22:20 and 2 Chronicles 34:28 promises that Josiah will be "gathered into thy grave in peace" — a peaceful death. 2 Kings 23:29-30 and 2 Chronicles 35:23-24 then narrate his violent battlefield death at Megiddo against Pharaoh Necho, shot by archers and carried back to Jerusalem to die. The prophecy contradicts the outcome.
contradictions.commentary:
Huldah's oracle to Josiah in 2 Kings 22:20 is delivered as divine speech: "I will gather thee unto thy fathers, and thou shalt be gathered into thy grave in peace." Less than two chapters later, the same Deuteronomistic narrator has Josiah killed in battle at Megiddo. The Chronicler reproduces both the oracle and the violent death in parallel. The contradiction sits inside the same book, told by the same narrator, who apparently saw no problem putting them next to each other.

The standard apologetic move, traceable from Keil and Delitzsch through Gleason Archer and more recently Iain Provan, redefines "in peace" to mean "before the disaster" rather than "non-violently." The oracle's substantive content is that Josiah will die before he witnesses the Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem — and that part is true. He dies in 609 BCE; Jerusalem falls in 587 BCE. Bashalom in Hebrew can mean "at peace with Yahweh" or "in covenant peace," not necessarily "in tranquil circumstances."

That reading has lexical support. Hebrew shalom does have a broader semantic range than English "peace." Marvin Sweeney in his OTL Kings volume concedes the harmonization is grammatically possible. But Sweeney and Mordechai Cogan with Hayim Tadmor in the AB volume both argue that this is post-hoc reinterpretation. The oracle, taken on its plain narrative-promise terms, predicted a peaceful death. The Chronicler felt this so strongly that 2 Chronicles 35:21-22 inserts an explanation: Josiah disobeyed God's word through Necho and was therefore killed. The Chronicler is essentially admitting that Huldah's oracle was conditional and Josiah forfeited the promise.

Ralph Klein in the Hermeneia 2 Chronicles volume reads this as classic Chronistic damage control — when the inherited Kings narrative creates a theological problem, the Chronicler invents an explanation. Sara Japhet in OTL agrees. This isn't a harmonization that the original Kings author intended; it's a later Chronistic patch.

Verdict: the bashalom-as-pre-disaster harmonization works grammatically but reads against the natural sense of the oracle. The Chronicler himself felt the contradiction and tried to fix it by attributing Josiah's death to his own disobedience. The plain reading of Huldah's oracle is broken by the plain reading of Josiah's death.

contradictions.question: Who succeeded Jehoiakim as king?
contradictions.summary: 2 Kings 24:6 records that Jehoiakim slept with his fathers and his son Jehoiachin reigned in his stead. Jeremiah 36:30 declares that Jehoiakim "shall have none to sit upon the throne of David" — meaning no son should succeed him.
contradictions.commentary:
2 Kings 24:6 gives the standard succession formula: Jehoiakim died, his son Jehoiachin took the throne. Jeremiah 36:30, in an earlier oracle pronounced against Jehoiakim for burning Jeremiah's scroll, says Yahweh has decreed Jehoiakim will have "none to sit upon the throne of David" — meaning no descendant will hold the Davidic monarchy.

The standard apologetic harmonization — Jack Lundbom in the AB volumes on Jeremiah, F.B. Huey in the NAC — argues Jehoiachin's three-month reign doesn't really count as "sitting upon the throne of David." Three months and ten days before exile to Babylon is a technicality, not a real reign. Walter Brueggemann in his Jeremiah commentary takes a similar line: the prophetic oracle envisages a substantive enthronement, which Jehoiachin never achieved before deportation.

There's something to this. Jehoiachin's reign was nominal. He was a teenager (per 2 Kings 24:8 — see id 299 for the age problem) who reigned for three months before Nebuchadnezzar carted him to Babylon. He never exercised meaningful royal authority. So Jeremiah's oracle might be loosely true if you read "throne" as substantive enthronement rather than formal succession.

But the harmonization runs into trouble. The text of 2 Kings 24:6 uses the exact formula it uses for every other Davidic succession — "reigned in his stead" (malak takhtaiw). Jehoiachin is enumerated in subsequent royal genealogies and the Chronicler counts him as a king. He sits on the throne of David in the technical, formal, narrative sense. Jack Lundbom and William Holladay both concede the Jeremiah oracle was either falsified by Jehoiachin's brief succession or required radical reinterpretation. Holladay in the Hermeneia Jeremiah volume reads it as a prophetic oracle that didn't quite come true and had to be theologically rescued by redefining "throne."

The deeper issue: 1 Chronicles 3:17-18 lists Jehoiachin's seven sons born in exile, and Matthew 1:11-12 puts Jehoiachin's son Shealtiel in Jesus' Davidic genealogy. The Davidic line ran through Jehoiakim's son, even into exile. Jeremiah's curse was either prematurely lifted or never literally fulfilled.

Verdict: the harmonization works by redefining "throne" as substantive rule, which the text doesn't stipulate. On the plain succession-language of 2 Kings 24:6, Jehoiakim was succeeded by his son — exactly what Jeremiah said wouldn't happen.

contradictions.question: How old was Jehoiachin when he began to reign?
contradictions.summary: 2 Kings 24:8 says Jehoiachin was eighteen years old when he began to reign, for three months. 2 Chronicles 36:9 says he was eight years old, for three months and ten days. Two ages, two reign-lengths, same king, same accession.
contradictions.commentary:
This is the kind of textual contradiction that even conservative scholarship has stopped pretending isn't there. 2 Kings 24:8 says eighteen. 2 Chronicles 36:9 says eight. Both numbers are presented as the age at accession. They can't both be right.

Gleason Archer's standard move in the Encyclopedia of Bible Difficulties — and the one Edwin Thiele, John Walton, and Andrew Hill follow — is to attribute the discrepancy to scribal error. The Hebrew letter representing ten (yod) was dropped from the Chronicles manuscript at some point in transmission, turning shemonah esreh (eighteen) into shemonah (eight). The LXX of 2 Chronicles 36:9 in some manuscripts reads eighteen, supporting the proposal that eighteen is original and the Chronicles MT figure is corrupt. The Syriac Peshitta and some Lucianic recensions also preserve eighteen.

This is one of the rare cases where critical and apologetic scholarship actually agree on diagnosis. Ralph Klein in Hermeneia, Sara Japhet in OTL, Mordechai Cogan and Hayim Tadmor in AB II Kings, and the standard apologists all converge: 2 Chronicles 36:9 contains a scribal error and eighteen is the original reading.

The disagreement is over what this means. The apologist treats it as a transmission glitch that doesn't affect the doctrine of inerrancy — because inerrancy is typically scoped to the autographs, not the received text. The critical scholar points out that the received Masoretic Text is what's canonical for Protestant Bibles, the autographs don't exist, and the discipline of textual criticism can recover earlier readings only approximately. The MT of 2 Chronicles 36:9 says eight. That's the text canonized.

The parallel three-months versus three-months-and-ten-days difference is harder to explain by scribal error — the Chronicles version has additional information ("and ten days") that wasn't in Kings. That's not corruption, that's expansion. The Chronicler had access to a different oral or written tradition with more granular regnal data, or he invented the detail for rhetorical effect.

Verdict: a real contradiction in the canonical text, conceded across the scholarly spectrum, harmonized only by appeal to a hypothetical correct autograph that doesn't exist. The MT says eight. Kings says eighteen. The received text contains the error.

contradictions.question: Did Zedekiah's eyes see the king of Babylon?
contradictions.summary: Jeremiah 34:3 prophesies that Zedekiah's eyes will behold the eyes of the king of Babylon. 2 Kings 25:7 (and the parallel Jeremiah 39:7) reports that the Babylonians put out Zedekiah's eyes before transporting him to Babylon — so he never sees the king of Babylon while in Babylon. The oracle and the fulfillment use the same anatomy in incompatible ways.
contradictions.commentary:
Jeremiah 34:3 says Zedekiah "shall behold the eyes of the king of Babylon" — face-to-face encounter. 2 Kings 25:7 narrates the fulfillment: "They slew the sons of Zedekiah before his eyes, and put out the eyes of Zedekiah, and bound him in fetters of brass, and carried him to Babylon." The pattern: Zedekiah witnesses his sons killed (eyes intact), then has his eyes gouged out, then is hauled to Babylon (no eyes).

The standard apologetic harmonization, defended by Walter Brueggemann, F.B. Huey, and Jack Lundbom in the AB Jeremiah volume, threads the needle technically: Zedekiah DID see the king of Babylon in person — Nebuchadnezzar at Riblah — BEFORE his eyes were put out. The order of events in 2 Kings 25:6-7 puts the face-to-face meeting before the blinding. So Jeremiah 34:3's prediction was fulfilled at Riblah, and the blinding came afterward. Ezekiel 12:13 even prophesies the same complex outcome: "I will bring him to Babylon... yet shall he not see it."

This harmonization actually works at the level of bare event-sequence. Zedekiah's eyes did behold Nebuchadnezzar's eyes at Riblah before being put out. That's the technical fulfillment. The narrative wasn't engineered after-the-fact to dissolve the contradiction; it's preserved in 2 Kings 25:6 prior to the blinding in 25:7. And Ezekiel 12:13 independently makes the same compound prediction.

Where this gets interesting is the literary effect. Lundbom and William Holladay both note the texts seem designed to highlight the prophetic tension. Zedekiah will see the king, AND Zedekiah will not see Babylon. The prophets are using the eye-imagery rhetorically — Jeremiah 34 emphasizes seeing as encounter, Ezekiel 12 emphasizes seeing as understanding/territorial knowledge. The narrative resolution in 2 Kings 25 satisfies both prophecies precisely because the prophecies were calibrated to be paradoxically fulfilled.

Verdict: this is one of the rare cases where the apologetic harmonization holds up. The sequence in 2 Kings 25:6-7 allows Zedekiah to see Nebuchadnezzar before his eyes are removed. Jeremiah 34:3 isn't contradicted by 2 Kings 25:7 — it's fulfilled in a deliberately constructed way. The contradiction is more apparent than real, surviving only if you read the prophecy in isolation from its narrative resolution.
